findings.title: Hardcoded credential in source
findings.description: A literal value is assigned to `refundSigningKey`. The value is committed to the repository and ships with every checkout, build artefact and container image.

evidence.note: Added line matched a security-sensitive pattern.

findings.whyItMatters: Git history is copied to every clone, CI cache and fork. Rotating a leaked key requires rotating the deployment, not just the file.
consequences: Credential reuse across environments
Unauthorised access with the developer's privileges
Secret remains recoverable from git history after deletion
findings.recommendation: Read the value from the environment or a secret manager, validate it at startup, and rotate the committed value. Removing the line alone does not revoke the secret.

findings.whyItMatters: Parameter binding is the only reliable separation between SQL syntax and data. Interpolation makes every caller of this function an injection surface.
consequences: Data exfiltration across tenants
Data modification or deletion
Authentication bypass when the query guards a login
findings.recommendation: Use bound parameters (`$1`, `?`, named parameters) and pass values separately. Never build query text from request data.

findings.title: Destructive schema change in migration
findings.description: The migration executes `ALTER TABLE payments DROP COLUMN legacy_reference;`. Existing rows and any deploy that still runs the previous schema version are affected.

evidence.snippet: + ALTER TABLE payments DROP COLUMN legacy_reference;

findings.whyItMatters: Migrations run before or during a rolling deploy; destructive DDL breaks old instances that are still serving traffic and cannot be undone by rolling back the application.
consequences: Data loss
Failed requests during the deploy window
Irreversible rollback
findings.recommendation: Use expand/contract: add the new column, dual-write, backfill, switch reads, then drop in a later release after a backup.

findings.whyItMatters: A customer or integration can request refunds above the merchant's configured limit. That is a direct money-loss path, and the documentation tells operators the control exists.

findings.title: Payment operation in router.post callback has no idempotency guard
findings.description: A money-moving call is performed without an idempotency key or a deduplication check visible in the same function.
findings.whyItMatters: Clients and gateways retry on timeout. Without a key, a retry is indistinguishable from a new instruction and the customer is charged twice.
consequences: Duplicate charges
Refund reconciliation work
Loss of customer trust
findings.recommendation: Accept a client-supplied idempotency key, persist it with a unique constraint before calling the provider, and return the stored result for repeats.

findings.title: calculateFee now rejects every non-EUR charge, breaking the charge path
findings.description: The new currency guard throws for any currency other than EUR. charge now calls calculateFee with request.amount.currency, so any existing non-EUR charge that used to succeed will now fail with a ValidationError. The change is not described as a behaviour change in the docs or agent notes.

evidence.note: Any currency other than EUR now throws inside the fee calculation.
charge passes the caller's currency, so non-EUR charges reach the new throw.

findings.whyItMatters: This is a runtime regression on the core charge endpoint, and it is not covered by the deterministic signature finding. Any merchant or storefront that charges in another currency will start failing.
consequences: Charges in non-EUR currencies return errors where they previously succeeded.
Checkout failures appear without any change to the charge request shape.
findings.reproduction: Call PaymentService.charge with amount.currency = 'USD'. calculateFee throws 'unsupported currency' before the payment is created.
findings.recommendation: Confirm whether non-EUR charges are supported today. If they are, keep the existing behaviour for them or gate the change behind a feature flag. Add a charge test for each supported currency.

findings.title: Error swallowed in refund
findings.description: An exception is caught and discarded without logging, rethrowing, or returning a failure result.
findings.whyItMatters: A swallowed error makes the operation look successful while its side effect never happened; callers commit state that the failed step never produced.
consequences: Silent data loss
Retries that never happen
Incidents without a stack trace
findings.recommendation: Handle the specific error you expect, and rethrow or wrap everything else preserving `cause`. If the failure is intentionally ignorable, log it with enough context to debug.

findings.title: Unserialised read-modify-write in refund
findings.description: `refund` reads a value, computes a new value in application code and writes it back (lines 82-111). No transaction, row lock, atomic update or version check appears in this function.
findings.whyItMatters: Two concurrent requests can both read the same starting value and both write a result derived from it, so one update is silently lost. The window is the time between the read and the write, which includes every `await`.
consequences: Lost updates under concurrent traffic
Balances or counters that drift from the ledger
Reconciliation failures that are hard to reproduce
findings.reproduction: Send two requests for the same record concurrently: both read value V, both write V+d, and the result is V+d instead of V+2d.
findings.recommendation: Make the mutation atomic: `UPDATE ... SET balance = balance + $1 ... RETURNING`, a `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` inside a transaction, or an optimistic version column with a retry on conflict.

findings.whyItMatters: Rollback is the only fast recovery path when a deploy fails after the schema change has been applied.
consequences: Schema/code mismatch after rollback
Manual database surgery during an incident
findings.recommendation: Add an explicit `down` migration, or document why the change is intentionally irreversible and how to recover from a backup.

findings.title: JSON parsed without a failure path
findings.description: `JSON.parse` is called in a function with no surrounding `try`/`catch`, so malformed input throws out of the handler.
findings.whyItMatters: Parsing throws `SyntaxError` on malformed input; without a guard the whole request fails as a 500 instead of a 400, and queue consumers retry forever.
consequences: 500 responses for client mistakes
Poison messages that block a queue partition
findings.recommendation: Parse inside a guard and validate the shape with a schema before using it; return a typed validation error.

findings.title: Synchronous I/O (readFileSync) added
findings.description: `readFileSync` blocks the event loop for the duration of the filesystem or process call.
findings.whyItMatters: Node.js serves all concurrent requests on one thread; every millisecond blocked here is added to every in-flight request.
consequences: Latency spikes under concurrent traffic
Health-check timeouts during cold disk or large files
findings.recommendation: Use the promise API (`fs/promises`) or stream the file; keep synchronous calls for CLI startup and tests.

findings.title: Undocumented environment variable: PAYMENT_REFUND_LIMIT
findings.description: `PAYMENT_REFUND_LIMIT` is read by the change but does not appear in any README, .env example, or deployment manifest in the repository.

evidence.note: Searched 19 repository files for "PAYMENT_REFUND_LIMIT"; no documentation match.

findings.whyItMatters: A required variable that exists only in the author's shell fails the first deploy to a clean environment, usually at startup or on the first request.
consequences: Failed deploys
Runtime errors only in environments the author never tested
findings.recommendation: Document the variable with a safe default in the README and .env.example, and fail fast at startup with a clear message when it is missing.

findings.title: Non-numeric PAYMENT_REFUND_LIMIT silently denies every refund
findings.description: Number() of a malformed environment value yields NaN. Every comparison against NaN is false, so isRefundAllowed rejects all refunds, and the failure is silent with no startup validation. Nothing in the excerpt validates the parsed limit.

evidence.note: A non-numeric env value produces NaN with no check.
With maxRefundCents = NaN, the comparison is always false, so every refund is denied.

findings.whyItMatters: Ledger totals can overstate what was settled after refunds. The refund stats are then wrong for reporting, which is the stated purpose of refund_stats.

findings.reproduction: Capture a payment, refund part of it, then run settleBatchAtomic for its batch. The ledger row carries the original amount_cents.
findings.recommendation: Either implement refund reconciliation in the settlement query, joining refunds, or correct docs/payments.md so it does not claim reconciliation that the code lacks. Add a settlement test that covers a partially refunded payment.

fixes.label: Option A — Pessimistic locking
fixes.description: Make the mutation atomic: `UPDATE ... SET balance = balance + $1 ... RETURNING`, a `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` inside a transaction, or an optimistic version column with a retry on conflict. Select the affected row with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` inside one transaction so concurrent callers serialise before reading.
advantages: Simple to reason about
No retry loop in application code
disadvantages: Holds row locks for the duration of the transaction
Throughput limited by lock contention on hot rows
fixes.performance: Serialises writers to the same row; read throughput is unaffected.
sideEffects: Long transactions can block other writers
Requires a connection per transaction
testing: Two concurrent transactions on the same row
Transaction rollback leaves no partial write
fixes.compatibility: Requires a database that supports row-level locks (PostgreSQL, MySQL/InnoDB).

fixes.label: Option B — Atomic update
fixes.description: Express the mutation as a single statement (`UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + $1 WHERE id = $2 RETURNING balance`) and validate the returned value.
advantages: No lock held in application code
One round-trip
Correct under any concurrency level
disadvantages: Business rules must fit in SQL
Harder to unit test without a database
fixes.performance: Best write throughput of the three options; one statement per operation.
sideEffects: Triggers and constraints must be understood before changing the statement
testing: Concurrent increments produce the exact expected total
Insufficient-funds path returns a typed error
fixes.compatibility: Portable across SQL databases with minor syntax differences (`RETURNING` is PostgreSQL-specific).

fixes.label: Option C — Optimistic versioning
fixes.description: Add a `version` column, read it with the row, and write with `WHERE version = $n`; retry when zero rows are affected.
advantages: No long-lived locks
Detects concurrent modification explicitly
disadvantages: Retry loop and backoff required
Schema change on the affected table
fixes.performance: Fast under low contention, retries under high contention.
sideEffects: Migration to add the column
Callers must handle a conflict error
testing: Second writer with a stale version is rejected

fixes.label: Option B — Restore original signature and add a separate currency-aware method
fixes.approach: Revert the exported signature and add a new method for validated, currency-aware fees
fixes.description: Restores calculateFee(amountCents) to its original single-argument form, which is the public contract. The currency check moves into a new method, calculateFeeForCurrency(amountCents, currency), which validates the currency and delegates to calculateFee. charge() switches to the new method. The original calculateFee body is assumed to be the EUR rate logic shown in the current file, because the pre-change body is not provided.
advantages: Restores the original exported contract, so all four external call sites keep working with no edits.
Keeps the currency guard in an explicit, separately named method, so the intent is visible at call sites.
Leaves room for per-currency pricing without changing the core fee function.
disadvantages: Adds a second public method to the class, which is new surface to document and maintain.

Assumes the original calculateFee body matched the EUR rate logic in the current file. If it differed, this change would alter fee results, and the limitation should be checked against the pre-change source.
Callers that adopt the new method must learn two entry points.
fixes.performance: Negligible. One extra method call per charge.
sideEffects: Any caller that wants currency validation must switch to calculateFeeForCurrency.
The original calculateFee no longer throws for non-EUR input, so out-of-band callers that relied on that throw would change behaviour.
testing: Unit test: calculateFee(1000) matches the pre-change value for the original signature.
Unit test: calculateFeeForCurrency(1000, 'EUR') equals calculateFee(1000).
Unit test: calculateFeeForCurrency(1000, 'USD') throws ValidationError.
Unit test: charge() with a EUR amount produces the same feeCents as before the change.
Typecheck all four external call sites against the restored signature.
fixes.compatibility: Restores the original exported signature exactly. Source- and behaviour-compatible for existing callers, subject to confirming the original body matches the current EUR logic.
